title: Tomas Learns to Roar
markdown:
In days the tide still remembers, salt wind came off the waves and found Tomas the badger at the grand doors of the Seaside Pavilion. The chairs waited in obedient rows. The velvet ropes hung as if they had been rehearsed. Tomas, civic choir arranger of some renown, believed joy was a symphony and that careful planning was its conductor. Today the pavilion would host his lecture on the sparkle of order, and he meant every lamp, every angle, every grain of sand to keep its appointed place.

His spectacles caught the sea and threw it back at him in two small, trembling lakes.

“Forty-five degrees,” he murmured, nudging a pebble off a rope as if the pebble had volunteered for mischief. “Even light. No sand on the boards.”

Yara the mole came up from a dip, fur still wet, smelling of kelp and good humour. She was older, and her nose knew both rich soil and the sort of afternoon that refused to sit still.

“Looking awfully spiffy, Tom,” she said, her voice like dry leaves deciding to dance. She bumped his elbow. “All set for the talk on how order makes life sparkle?”

Tomas straightened the round glasses. Sunlight shivered in them.

“Every detail is accounted for. The joy of a well-organised event is paramount. It prevents… tangents.”

Yara’s wink was a bright bead. She tapped the glass of his spectacles with one damp claw, and the little lakes rippled.

“Wish for a still pond,” she said, almost singing,
“and the tide will write its own song.”

The first boon arrived as wind. It swept into the open pavilion like a guest who had never learned to knock, snatched the colour-coded seating chart from Tomas’s paws, and sent the papers skating across the boards. Early arrivals gasped. Then a ripple of amusement moved through them, as if the room had been waiting for an entrance.

A plump robin in a tiny waistcoat chuckled.

“The plan is still excellent. Reality is simply being overfamiliar today.”

Tomas’s whiskers twitched. A busy squirrel now shared a seat with a very surprised hedgehog. He had grouped attendees by affinity. He had planned social flow. This was not flow. This was weather.

“Don’t you worry,” Yara called, retrieving a sheet that had landed, rather comically, on her head. “Overture, darling. Anticipation makes the main performance sweeter.”

Tomas looked into a puddle the wind had left on the floor. His own face jumped there, rearranged by every small wave. He wanted to snatch the papers back into their rainbow order. Instead he let Yara stack them crookedly against a chair, because the robin was already seating himself wherever the breeze had suggested, and the hedgehog, after a startled moment, had begun to share a biscuit.

The second boon woke in the walls. Tomas had just begun his rehearsed introduction when the pavilion’s ancient sound system crackled to life, not with the quiet of gentle waves he had chosen, but with a rollicking sea shanty. The audience, whom he had imagined listening in calm rows, burst into foot-stomping. A few of the more spirited attendees began to sway.

Heat climbed Tomas’s neck. His atmosphere of contemplation was being jigged to pieces. Yet Yara’s smile was genuine, and she hummed. The robin tapped. A large, jolly seal clapped his flippers until the rhythm had a second heartbeat.

“Marvelous!” the seal boomed. “A real taste of the seaside spirit!”

Tomas took a breath that tasted of salt and old varnish. In the dark glass of a window, the whole pavilion repeated itself: stamping feet, crooked chairs, a badger at a podium trying not to look like a man whose score had grown extra notes.

“A spirited start,” he managed, “to our discussion.”

The plan is still excellent, the robin’s line seemed to say, even as the shanty refused to sit down.

The third boon came on white wings. Seagulls took the stage with uninhibited glee and left their own abstract comments on the wooden podium and on Tomas’s notes. He stared. His presentation, that monument to pristine planning, was now decorated.

There were no groans. Children pointed and giggled. Adults chuckled. One fluffy gull, with a rakish tilt to his head, preened as if he had been engaged for the interval. A wise-looking owl on a rafter called it nature’s own abstract art, and the room, which had already learned how to laugh, learned how to look.

Tomas stood in salt air and seagull perfume. The seating chart was a memory. The notes were smudged. A stripe of late sun found a faintly singed scrap he had tried to sweep away, and lit the chalk dust he had raised in that hurried, useless clearing. The sea beyond the doors kept offering him its bright, ungovernable mirror.

Yara, in the front row, gave him a thumbs-up that was all earth and tide.

Something in him shifted, not with a speech, but with the simple fact of the room as it was. He straightened his spectacles. The two little lakes of glass showed him people who had already begun without permission.

“I thought joy lived in every note in its place,” he said, and the shanty, now softer, seemed to wait for him. “Every voice in harmony. Every seat exactly so.” He gestured at the pavilion, at the squirrel still companionably close to the hedgehog, at the gull who had become, against every rule, a guest. “Perhaps it also lives in being here. In letting the music play even when it is not the tune we marked.”

He spoke then of rhythm and of shared work, not of angles. The audience listened to a badger finding his own time. When he finished, applause filled the high ceiling — not for a lecture on order, but for an afternoon that had gone off the map and found, somehow, a chorus.

Outside, the tide kept writing. Tomas tucked the singed scrap into his waistcoat. From the rafters the robin’s line still hung, as catchy as a chorus anyone could join:

The plan is still excellent.
